title: China’s RiboX Unveils First Human Data on Circular RNA Therapies, Marking Biotech Breakthrough
body:
A landmark study published in the New England Journal of Medicine has confirmed that a circular RNA (circRNA) therapeutic developed by Boston‑area biotech RiboX Therapeutics can significantly improve salivary flow in patients suffering from xerostomia, a chronic dry‑mouth condition that affects millions worldwide. The investigational drug, designated RXRG001, demonstrated measurable increases in unstimulated saliva production and reported symptom relief, marking the first human data for a circRNA‑based therapy and positioning RiboX ahead of rivals such as Orna Therapeutics, Orbital Therapeutics and Sail Biomedicines in the race to commercialise the next generation of RNA medicines.

The phase 1/2 trial enrolled 48 adults with moderate to severe xerostomia, most of whom had developed the condition as a side‑effect of radiation therapy for head‑and‑neck cancers. Participants received a single intraglandular injection of RXRG001, a synthetic circRNA construct engineered to express a secreted protein that stimulates the remaining salivary gland tissue. Over a 12‑week follow‑up period, the treatment group showed a 45 percent rise in unstimulated whole‑mouth saliva volume compared with baseline, while placebo recipients exhibited no meaningful change. Patient‑reported outcomes mirrored the objective data, with a majority indicating reduced oral dryness, improved taste perception and better overall quality of life.

Circular RNA, unlike its linear messenger RNA counterpart, forms a covalently closed loop that renders it resistant to exonuclease degradation. This structural stability translates into longer intracellular persistence and sustained protein production, potentially allowing lower dosing frequencies than conventional mRNA vaccines and therapeutics. RiboX’s platform exploits these attributes by delivering circRNA directly into target tissues using a lipid nanoparticle carrier, a method that has been refined over the past five years through collaborations with academic laboratories and contract manufacturing organisations. The successful translation of pre‑clinical efficacy into human benefit suggests that circRNA could overcome several limitations that have hampered broader adoption of mRNA‑based drugs, such as rapid clearance and the need for repeated administrations.

The implications of the study extend beyond xerostomia. Industry analysts note that the same circRNA technology could be adapted to a wide array of indications, ranging from protein‑replacement therapies for rare genetic disorders to oncology applications where sustained expression of immunomodulatory proteins is desirable. RiboX has already filed patents covering circRNA constructs for enzyme replacement in lysosomal storage diseases and for cytokine delivery in solid tumours. If the company can replicate the safety and efficacy signals seen in the current trial, it could open a new therapeutic class that competes directly with both mRNA platforms and traditional viral vector approaches.

Financial backing for circRNA research has surged in recent years, with venture capital and pharmaceutical partners collectively allocating billions of dollars to three Boston‑region startups—RiboX, Orna and Orbital—each vying to be the first to market a clinically validated product. While Orna recently announced promising data for a circRNA vaccine against influenza, and Orbital disclosed early pre‑clinical results for a circRNA‑encoded antibody, RiboX’s NEJM publication provides the most concrete evidence of human benefit to date. The company’s lead investor, a major global pharmaceutical conglomerate, has pledged an additional $250 million to accelerate late‑stage development and scale up manufacturing capacity.

Looking ahead, RiboX plans to launch a larger, double‑blind, multicenter phase 3 trial later this year, enrolling a more diverse patient population and testing repeated dosing schedules. Success in that study could pave the way for regulatory approval and, ultimately, commercial launch, potentially establishing circRNA as a viable alternative to mRNA for a spectrum of chronic diseases. As the field of RNA therapeutics matures, the emergence of circular RNA may redefine the balance between efficacy, durability and convenience, offering patients and clinicians a new tool in the fight against conditions that have long lacked effective treatments.
